The largest cities of [South Korea](South_Korea "South Korea") have an autonomous status equivalent to that of provinces. <Seoul>, the largest city and capital, is classified as a *teukbyeolsi* ([Special City](List_of_special_cities_of_South_Korea "List of special cities of South Korea")), while the next six-largest cities are classified as *gwangyeoksi* (Metropolitan Cities). Smaller cities are classified as *si* ("cities") and are under provincial jurisdiction, at the same level as counties.

## City status

Article 10 of the Local Autonomy Act defines the standards under which a populated area may become a city: an area which is predominantly [urbanised](Urban_area "Urban area") and has a population of at least 50,000; a *[gun](Gun_(administrative_division) "Gun (administrative division)")* which has an urbanised area with a population of at least 50,000; or a *gun* which has a total population of at least 150,000 and multiple urbanised areas each with a population of at least 20,000.[[1]](List_of_cities_in_South_Korea#cite_note-LocalAutonomyAct-1) Cases outside of these standards require specific legislation, such as the special bill by the [National Assembly](National_Assembly_(South_Korea) "National Assembly (South Korea)") to designate <Gyeryong> as a city.

Under Article 3 of the Local Autonomy Act, a city with a population of less than 500,000 may create administrative subdivisions in the form of *[dong](Dong_(administrative_division) "Dong (administrative division)")* in its urbanised area and *[eup](Eup_(administrative_division) "Eup (administrative division)")* or *[myeon](Myeon_(administrative_division) "Myeon (administrative division)")* in its rural area, while a city with a population of more than 500,000 may create administrative subdivisions in the form of non-autonomous *[gu](Gu_(administrative_division) "Gu (administrative division)")*.[[2]](List_of_cities_in_South_Korea#cite_note-2)

## Classifications for large municipal cities

The national government can designate cities of at least 500,000 inhabitants as special status cities. This status expands the scope of administrative authority delegated from the provincial government to the city government.[[3]](List_of_cities_in_South_Korea#cite_note-Article198-3) There is no legal standard for becoming a [metropolitan city](Special_cities_of_South_Korea "Special cities of South Korea"), but it was usually promoted to a metropolitan city when the population was close to 1,000,000. However, considering that there are four cities in <Suwon>, <Changwon>, <Goyang>, and <Yongin> that have a population of more than 1 million but have not become metropolitan cities, there is no further promotion.

### Big city

A **big city** is a city (other than a special city or a metropolitan city) that has a population greater than 500,000, and has been designated by an order of the national government under Article 198 of the Local Autonomy Act. Big municipal cities are given the power to subdivide themselves into [non-autonomous districts](List_of_districts_in_South_Korea "List of districts in South Korea") (일반구; 一般區).[[3]](List_of_cities_in_South_Korea#cite_note-Article198-3) However, some big municipal cities have chosen not to divide themselves into districts, such as <Bucheon>, <Gimhae>, [Hwaseong](Hwaseong%2C_Gyeonggi "Hwaseong, Gyeonggi"), or <Namyangju>. Currently, South Korea has a total of 17 big cities. "Specific city" (특정시, 特定市) is an unofficial term for big city with municipal status.

Due its legal status as an administrative city, [Jeju City](Jeju_City "Jeju City") cannot be designated as a "big city" under the Local Autonomy Law, despite having an estimated population exceeding 500,000 as of 2022. The designation of "administrative city" was created by the law which granted special self-governing status to [Jeju Province](Jeju_Province "Jeju Province"); that law specifically states that the Local Autonomy Act would not apply to administrative cities. As such, [Jeju City](Jeju_City "Jeju City") does not enjoy special autonomy and only has the same legal powers as the much smaller <Seogwipo> City. The administrative authority of [Jeju City](Jeju_City "Jeju City") is trying to expand the scope of administrative authority delegated from the provincial government to the city government.[[4]](List_of_cities_in_South_Korea#cite_note-4)

### Special-status city

A **special-status city** is a subclass of big municipal city that has a population greater than 1,500,000.

### Other sects

Apart from Cheondoism, other sects based on [indigenous religion](Indigenous_religion "Indigenous religion") were founded between the end of the 19th century and the early decades of the 20th century. They include <Daejongism> (대종교 *Daejonggyo*),[[108]](Religion_in_South_Korea#cite_note-110) which has as its central creed the worship of Dangun, legendary founder of <Gojoseon>, thought of as the first proto-Korean kingdom; and a splinter sect of Cheondoism: <Suwunism>.

<Jeungsanism> (증산교 *Jeungsangyo*) defines a family of religions founded in the early 20th century[[109]](Religion_in_South_Korea#cite_note-111) that emphasise magical practices and [millenarian](Millenarianism "Millenarianism") teachings of [Kang Jeungsan](Kang_Jeungsan "Kang Jeungsan") ([Gang Il-Sun](Gang_Il-Sun "Gang Il-Sun")). There are more than a hundred "Jeungsan religions," including the now defunct <Bocheonism>: the largest in Korea is currently [Daesun Jinrihoe](Daesun_Jinrihoe "Daesun Jinrihoe") (대순진리회), an offshoot of the still existing Taegeukdo (태극도), while <Jeungsando> (증산도) is the most active overseas.[[110]](Religion_in_South_Korea#cite_note-112)

There are also a number of small religious sects, which have sprung up around <Gyeryongsan> ("Rooster-Dragon Mountain", always one of Korea's most-sacred areas) in [South Chungcheong Province](South_Chungcheong_Province "South Chungcheong Province"), the supposed future site of the founding of a new dynasty originally prophesied in the 18th century (or before). Japanese <Tenriism> (천리교 *Cheonligyo*) also claims to have thousands of South Korean members.[[111]](Religion_in_South_Korea#cite_note-113)

According to Andrew Eungi Kim, there was a rise of new religious movements in the late 1900s which account for about 10 percent of all churches in South Korea. According to Kim, this is the outcome of foreign invasions, as well as conflicting views regarding social and political issues. Many of the new religious movements are [syncretic](Religious_syncretism "Religious syncretism") in character.[[112]](Religion_in_South_Korea#cite_note-114)

### Confucianism

Main article: [Korean Confucianism](Korean_Confucianism "Korean Confucianism")

Only few contemporary South Koreans identify as adherents of Confucianism (유교 *Yugyo*). Korean intellectuals historically developed a distinct [Korean Confucianism](Korean_Confucianism "Korean Confucianism").[[114]](Religion_in_South_Korea#cite_note-116)[[115]](Religion_in_South_Korea#cite_note-Koh192-117) However, with the end of the Joseon state and the wane of Chinese influence in the 19th and 20th century, Confucianism was abandoned. The influence of Confucian ethical thought remains strong in other religious practices, and in [Korean culture](Korean_culture "Korean culture") in general. Confucian rituals are still practised at various times of the year. The most prominent of these are the annual rites held at the [Shrine of Confucius](Munmyo "Munmyo") in Seoul. Other rites, for instance those in honour of clan founders, are held at shrines found throughout the country.[[116]](Religion_in_South_Korea#cite_note-118)[[117]](Religion_in_South_Korea#cite_note-119)

### Hinduism

Main article: [Hinduism in Korea](Hinduism_in_Korea "Hinduism in Korea")

See also: [List of Hindu temples in South Korea](List_of_Hindu_temples_in_South_Korea "List of Hindu temples in South Korea")

Hinduism (힌두교 *Hindugyo*) is practiced among South Korea's small [Indian](India "India"), [Nepali](Nepal "Nepal") and [Balinese](Bali "Bali") migrant community. However, Hindu traditions such as [yoga](Yoga "Yoga") and <Vedanta> have attracted interest among younger South Koreans. Hindu temples in the Korea include the [Sri Radha Shyamasundar Mandir](Sri_Radha_Shyamasundar_Mandir "Sri Radha Shyamasundar Mandir") in central Seoul, [Sri Lakshmi Narayanan Temple](Sri_Lakshmi_Narayanan_Temple "Sri Lakshmi Narayanan Temple") in metropolitan Seoul, [Himalayan Meditation and Yoga Sadhana Mandir](Himalayan_Meditation_and_Yoga_Sadhana_Mandir "Himalayan Meditation and Yoga Sadhana Mandir") in <Seocho> in Seoul, and [Sri Sri Radha Krishna temple](Sri_Sri_Radha_Krishna_temple "Sri Sri Radha Krishna temple") in <Uijeongbu> 20 km away on outskirt of Seoul.[[118]](Religion_in_South_Korea#cite_note-120)

### Islam

Main article: [Islam in Korea](Islam_in_Korea "Islam in Korea")

Islam (이슬람교 *Iseullamgyo*) in South Korea is represented by a community of roughly 40,000 [Muslims](Muslim "Muslim"), mainly composed by people who converted during the [Korean War](Korean_War "Korean War") and their descendants and not including migrant workers from South and Southeast Asia. The largest mosque is the [Seoul Central Mosque](Seoul_Central_Mosque "Seoul Central Mosque") in the <Itaewon> district of Seoul; smaller mosques can be found in most of the country's major cities. There are around a hundred thousand foreign workers from Muslim countries, particularly Indonesians, Malaysians, Pakistanis and Bangladeshis.[[119]](Religion_in_South_Korea#cite_note-121)

### Judaism

Main article: [History of the Jews in South Korea](History_of_the_Jews_in_South_Korea "History of the Jews in South Korea")

The Jewish existence in South Korea effectively began with the dawn of the Korean War in 1950. At this time a large number of Jewish soldiers, including the chaplain [Chaim Potok](Chaim_Potok "Chaim Potok"), came to the Korean peninsula. Today the Jewish community is very small and limited to the [Seoul Capital Area](Seoul_Capital_Area "Seoul Capital Area"). There have been very few Korean converts to Judaism (유대교 *Yudaegyo*).

### Shinto

Main article: [Shinto in Korea](Shinto_in_Korea "Shinto in Korea")

During Japan's colonisation of Korea (1910–1945), given the suggested common origins of the two peoples, Koreans were considered to be outright part of the Japanese population, to be wholly assimilated. The Japanese studied and coopted native *[Sindo](Korean_shamanism "Korean shamanism")* by overlapping it with their [State Shinto](State_Shinto "State Shinto") (similar measures of assimilation were applied to Buddhism), which hinged upon the worship of Japanese high gods and the emperor's godhead. Hundreds of Japanese [Shinto shrines](Shinto_shrines "Shinto shrines") were built throughout the peninsula.[[120]](Religion_in_South_Korea#cite_note-122) This policy led to massive conversion of Koreans to Christian churches, which were already well ingrained in the country, representing a concern for the Japanese program, and supported Koreans' independence.[[121]](Religion_in_South_Korea#cite_note-123) After the Allied forces defeated Japan in 1945, Korea was liberated from Japanese rule. As soon as the Shinto priests withdrew to Japan, all Shinto shrines in Korea were either destroyed or converted into another use.

### Sikhism

Main article: [Sikhism in South Korea](Sikhism_in_South_Korea "Sikhism in South Korea")

[Sikhs](Sikhism "Sikhism") have been in [South Korea](South_Korea "South Korea") for 50 years. The first South Korean [gurdwara](Gurdwara "Gurdwara") was established in 2001.[[122]](Religion_in_South_Korea#cite_note-124) There are about 550 Sikhs in South Korea, now recently the Sikhs in South were allowed to acquire South Korean citizenship.[[123]](Religion_in_South_Korea#cite_note-125)

The provincial capital is at <Changwon>. It is adjacent to the major metropolitan center and port of <Busan>. The UNESCO [World Heritage Site](World_Heritage_Site "World Heritage Site") <Haeinsa>, a [Buddhist temple](Korean_Buddhist_temples "Korean Buddhist temples") that houses the *[Tripitaka Koreana](Tripitaka_Koreana "Tripitaka Koreana")* and tourist attraction, is located in this province. ## Etymology

The name derives from [Korean](Korean_language "Korean language")  *Gyeongsang* 'joyous furthermore'; from  *gyeong (Korean [경](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/경 "wikt:경"), Hanja [慶](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/慶 "wikt:慶"))* 'celebrate', and  *sang (Korean [상](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/상 "wikt:상"), Hanja [尚](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/尚 "wikt:尚"))* 'append to'.
